summary:
Sort the weights. The heaviest hiker needs a boat now; give them the lightest hiker as a partner if the pair fits
(if even the lightest doesn't fit, nobody does). Either way the heaviest leaves. Two pointers do this in one pass
after sorting: O(n log n).

question.md:
Each boat carries at most **two** hikers with total weight at most `limit`. Everyone weighs at most `limit`.
Return the fewest boats.

- **Two per boat at most**, even if three light hikers would fit by weight.
- **Up to 10⁵ hikers.**

think.md:
Weights `[70, 50, 80, 50, 30, 90]`, limit 100. Sorted: `[30, 50, 50, 70, 80, 90]`. Trips: 90, 80, 70+30, 50+50: **4** boats.

The heaviest hiker is the hardest to pair. If the lightest hiker can join them, pairing those two is never
worse than any other plan (swap partners in any optimal plan and it stays valid). If the lightest can't join,
nobody can, so the heaviest rides alone. Either way, decide the heaviest and repeat.

approaches.title: Heaviest takes the heaviest partner who fits

idea.md: Sort descending. Repeatedly take the heaviest remaining hiker and scan the rest for the heaviest partner who still fits; remove both (or just the one).

build: For each untaken hiker, scan forward for the first untaken partner that fits.

lines.text: Heaviest first, with a mark for hikers already on a boat.

notes.java: Sorted ascending and walked from the end, which is the same as heaviest first.
notes.c: Sorted ascending and walked from the end, which is the same as heaviest first.

lines.text: The heaviest hiker still waiting gets a new boat.
The heaviest waiting hiker who still fits joins them.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²)** for the partner scans. **Space O(n).**

steps.text: 90 takes a boat alone: nobody left fits with them.
80 takes a boat alone: nobody left fits with them.

walk.title: Heaviest first: each heaviest hiker takes the heaviest remaining partner that still fits (scanning everyone left).

limits.md: The partner scan is wasted effort: if any partner fits the heaviest hiker, the lightest one does, and pairing with the lightest is just as good. That makes it two pointers.

approaches.title: Sort, then pair heaviest with lightest

idea.md: Sort ascending; `i` at the lightest, `j` at the heaviest. Each boat takes hiker `j`, plus hiker `i` if `a[i] + a[j] ≤ limit`. Move the pointers and count.

build: While `i ≤ j`: if the pair fits, `i += 1`; always `j −= 1`; count a boat.

lines.text: `i` at the lightest waiting hiker, `j` at the heaviest.
While anyone is waiting (`i == j` is a single last hiker).
If the lightest fits with the heaviest, they share. (When `i == j`, this just moves `i` past the same hiker, which is harmless.)
The heaviest leaves on this boat either way.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log n)** for the sort; the pairing pass is O(n). **Space O(n)** for the sorted copy.

steps.text: Heaviest 70 and lightest 30 share a boat (100 ≤ 100).
Heaviest 50 and lightest 50 share a boat (100 ≤ 100).

walk.title: Sort. The heaviest hiker must go now; pair them with the lightest if the two fit, since the lightest is the best partner anyone could have.

takeaways.md:
- **Pairing greedy:** the hardest item (heaviest) takes the most accommodating partner (lightest), or goes alone.
- Sorting turns "find the best partner" into moving two pointers.
- Exchange arguments justify greedy pairings: swapping partners in any optimal plan never makes it worse.
